data: Composer skill: The skill that teaches an agent to assemble CircleCI jobs into a correct workflow layout, and to check it with the planner tools. Compose eval: Three cases that test whether an agent with the composer skill composes a correct workflow, graded by a script with no model involved.

Can an agent with the workflow composer skill assemble CircleCI jobs into a correct workflow? Each case gives it the demo’s job definitions (jobs.yml, the demo’s continue.yml without its workflows) and a goal. It answers with a complete config: the jobs as given, plus the workflows: it composed.
check.sh then judges each answer, with no model involved:
circleci config validate; circleci-smarter layout check, with mandatory security-scan and restricted context deploy; circleci-smarter policy check against policies/; the case’s own assertions (which jobs must be in it, and in what order). Case Goal 1 compose the full workflow for main and branches, from scratch 2 compose the smallest correct workflow for a set of selected jobs 3 repair a broken layout (case-3-broken.yml) from the checker’s findings The results of the first run are in the validation page, and the answers are in answers/.

You wire jobs that already exist into workflows. You do not write jobs, steps or orbs. Load the CircleCI MCP skill write-config first (get_skill with skill: "write-config", then reference: "references/orbs.md"): it covers orbs, functions and validate_config. This skill adds only the workflow layer.
Tags such as cfg#requires name the source of a rule; the URLs are at the end. (heuristic) marks advice that is not a documented rule.
data.hard-rules#Hard rules:
Layout
Add no job except approvals, no-op coordinators and the gate. Use catalog names verbatim. One entry per job, or distinct name: values. cfg#name Write only keys that the references or the docs list. A misspelled key on a local job fails to compile; on an orb job it can be ignored without a word (write-config skill). Every requires item is an entry of the same workflow: its name:, a matrix alias or a job-group name. No cycle. The compiler rejects the rest. cfg#requires cfg#matrix-requires A required job that does not run is ignored, and a job whose requirements are all filtered out does not run either. Work this out for every filtered job and every approval. cfg#requires Statuses are success, failed, canceled, unauthorized, not_run and terminal. A job that requires X: failed or X: terminal gets the filters of X: the docs do not say what happens when X is filtered out. (heuristic) cfg#requires Approvals, contexts, mandatory jobs
An approval is type: approval on a workflow entry, with a unique name and no steps. Every job after it requires it. Place it after all checks, directly before the first job that must not run unapproved. wf#approval An approval and every job behind it carry the same filters. Filter only the approval and the job runs unapproved; filter only the job and the workflow waits on hold. cfg#requires wf#approval Keep the contexts the catalog gives a job and add none it does not need; with several, later ones win. ctx#combine A restricted context goes only on the jobs the bundle lists, behind an approval, with filters.branches.only in map form. Keep such jobs out of job groups. ctx#approve (policies/guardrails.rego) Mandatory jobs are plain entries (not in a job group), unfiltered, with no requires unless they need another job’s output, so no earlier failure keeps them from running. cfg#requires (policies/guardrails.rego) Gate
The gate is type: no-op with no filters. It requires every check job, directly or through coordinators, and nothing behind the approval, nor any cleanup or notify job. At least one of its requirements always runs. cook#gate cfg#requires Data
A job that attaches a workspace is downstream of every job it needs data from. Concurrent producers persist disjoint paths. A cache never carries this run’s output between jobs. ws#overview cache#race Conditions
Conditions read pipeline values and parameters, never environment variables. Never put << >> inside a bare expression. A when step takes a logic statement, not an expression. cfg#logic cook#when Speed and cost
Put the quickest jobs first, and add an edge only for a reason: a needless edge lengthens the critical path. wf#examples support#workflow-review Use serial-group for deploys and other shared state, and max_auto_reruns only for jobs known to be flaky. cfg#serial-group rerun#wf Planner v0.1
Prefer what the planner can evaluate: map branch and tag filters, and requires by success. A matrix, an expression filter, a non-literal workflow when or another status makes it run more, or leaves a job out of the gate. (docs/spec/v0.1.md steps 1, 5, 6; docs/limitations.md)

Never print environment variables or secrets.
data.which-reference-to-read#Which reference: When you Read wire requires, use a status, filter a job or an approval, use a matrix or a job group references/requires-and-statuses.md shape the graph: fan-out, coordinator, gate, fail fast, critical path, approval, deploy, serial-group, reruns references/shaping-patterns.md write when, unless, filters or step conditions references/conditions.md fix an order because of workspaces, caches or artifacts references/data-flow.md call a tool or read a finding references/tools.md want a complete, valid layout to copy examples/ Examples, each validated with circleci config validate: 01-small.yml (parallel checks, one build, a gate); 02-medium-fanout-workspaces.yml (workspaces, fan-out, a matrix by alias); 03-deploy-gated.yml (approval, restricted context, serial-group, cleanup, notify, gate).
data.workflow#Workflow: Read the catalog. For each selected job note its kind (build, approval, no-op, release), what it persists or attaches, its contexts and filters, matrix or parameters, orb or local. Copy names exactly. Mark the mandatory jobs and every job that uses a restricted context. If a job you need is not listed, stop and report it. Decide the stages. Everything runs in parallel unless an edge has a reason: a data contract (a consumer attaches what a producer persists), fail fast (cheap before expensive), policy (a restricted context needs an approval), order of effect (deploy after every check), shared state (serial-group). Usual order: cheap checks and the mandatory scan as roots, build, expensive checks, gate, approval, deploy, cleanup and notify. Wire requires. Fan out from producers. Collapse N×M with a no-op coordinator. Require a matrix by its alias and a job group by its name. Use a status other than success only on cleanup, notify and rollback jobs. Add conditions. Filters, workflow when, step when. Give an approval and the jobs behind it the same filters. Add the gate. One type: no-op job named smarter-gate, with no filters, that requires every check job and nothing behind the approval. It is the single required status check. Check the whole file, in this order: circleci config validate FILE, circleci-smarter layout check ..., circleci-smarter policy check ... (commands: references/tools.md §4 and §5). Repair. Read each finding’s code and message (references/tools.md §4 maps a finding to a fix), fix the cause in the layout, and run all three checks again. If a finding survives three repairs, stop and report it. Never pass a check by weakening the layout: do not drop a mandatory job, an approval, a context restriction or a branch filter, and do not edit policies/. Report the layout in a few lines, the result of each check, and what you could not verify. Leave everything outside the workflow you compose (other workflows, jobs, orbs, comments) as it was.

data: Benchmarks: Overview of end-to-end CI savings, historical backtest recall, and local performance targets for the planner and trace scripts. Performance benchmarks: Planner and trace-script timing on synthetic workloads, how the numbers were taken, and how to rerun them locally. Backtest: Recall and job-time savings when the planner is replayed against historical CI runs, and the limits of that replay.

The backtest command replays historical CI runs against today’s impact map and reports how often select mode would still have run failing jobs (recall) and how much job time it would have skipped (savings).
data.command#Command:
circleci-smarter backtest \ --history history.json \ --map impact-map.json.gz \ --config .circleci/continue.yml \ --workflow ci \ --parameters pipeline-params.json \ --mandatory security-scan \ --format md --parameters is a JSON object of pipeline parameter values, applied to every commit unless a history record carries its own parameters object. Use the same file you would pass to plan --parameters when the continuation config gates workflows or jobs on << pipeline.parameters.* >>.
--format json writes the machine-readable report (used for golden tests).
data.history-file-format#History file format:
A JSON array of commits:
[ { "commit": "sha", "base": "merge-base sha", "branch": "feature/x", "changed": [{ "path": "pkg/foo.go", "status": "M" }], "jobs": [ { "name": "go-test", "status": "failed", "duration_s": 120.5 } ] } ] Optional per-commit parameters overrides the --parameters file for that pipeline (same semantics as plan --parameters).
Build a history file with scripts/bench/fetch-history.sh (needs a CircleCI API token and a git clone). Fixture parsing is tested by scripts/bench/test-parse.sh.
data.limits-of-replay#Limits of replay: One map for all commits. The map reflects the repo layout at its revision (usually recent main). Older commits that touched different paths or job names are approximate. Changed files only. History carries a file list, not full git trees. Adds/deletes may miss directory moves the live planner would see via git ls-tree. Workflow drift. Failures in jobs removed from the config or renamed are unmatched (listed separately, not in recall). Savings count only jobs present in today’s workflow. Parameter gates. Without --parameters, workflow when expressions that depend on pipeline parameters may be unknown, which forces a full run and makes savings look like 0%. No guardrail replay. Backtest does not pass --policy-bundle; historical guardrail repairs are not simulated. Flaky detection depends on CircleCI job rerun metadata when history is mined; hand-written fixtures set "flaky": true explicitly. Use backtest to compare maps and tuning over time, not as a guarantee for every past commit.
data.measured-this-repository-2026-11-15#Meas:
Replayed 79 commits from the project’s ci workflow against the impact map from main at commit 83d7d6082:
Metric Value Failures (non-flaky) 5 Caught 5 Misses 0 Flaky (excluded) 0 Recall 100% Historical job time 13 737 s Would have skipped 949 s Savings 6.9% History here is mostly Go and .circleci/ changes, which reach most jobs, so skipped time stays small. Replaying the demo monorepo history would not measure much: those pipelines already ran in select mode when the traces were taken.
data.method#Method:
For each record in a history file, the planner runs in select mode with the recorded base, commit, branch, and changed paths. That reuses internal/planner exactly as plan --mode select does; backtest does not duplicate selection logic.
For each job that ran in CI:
Outcome Meaning Caught The job failed and select mode would still run it. Miss The job failed and select mode would skip it. Unmatched The job failed but its name is not in today’s workflow (renamed or removed); excluded from recall. Flaky The job failed then passed on a rerun of the same commit; excluded from recall. Recall is caught / (caught + misses) over non-flaky failures in jobs that still exist in the config.
Savings sums duration_s over matched jobs that ran historically but would be skipped, divided by matched recorded job time. Unmatched job time is reported separately.
data.scheduled-benchmark-on-main#Scheduled be: The benchmark workflow in .circleci/continue.yml runs when pipeline.trigger.type is schedule (the schedule is configured on the project in CircleCI, not in this file). It uses the smarter-workflows-ai context so fetch-history.sh can call the API with << pipeline.project.slug >> (GitHub App projects use the circleci/org/project form). It restores the latest impact map cache, fetches the last 200 ci pipelines, runs backtest, and stores backtest.md and backtest.json as artifacts.

data: Contributing: How to report a bug, propose a change and open a pull request for Smarter Workflows, a CircleCI Labs project. Security policy: How to report a vulnerability, and which versions get fixes.

Thank you for helping to improve Smarter Workflows, a CircleCI Labs project. Field engineers review issues and pull requests on a best-effort basis, with no SLA. Report a security problem by email, not in an issue (SECURITY.md).
data.commit-messages#Commit messages:
Use Conventional Commits: type(scope): summary. Keep each commit small and atomic.
Type Use for feat A new capability, or a changed command, flag or file format fix A bug fix docs Documentation only test Tests only ci The CircleCI pipeline chore Maintenance with no user-visible change refactor, perf Code changes that keep behavior, or improve speed A breaking change adds ! after the type or scope (feat(plan)!: rename a flag), or a BREAKING CHANGE: footer that says what the user has to change.
data.development#Development:
Requirements: Go (the version in go.mod), and the CircleCI CLI, which the tests use to validate every config that the planner generates. Set REQUIRE_CIRCLECI_CLI=1 to make a missing CLI fail the tests instead of skipping them.
gofmt -l . go vet ./... go test ./... circleci policy test policies scripts/test-trace.sh The commands check formatting (the output must be empty), vet, the Go tests, the Rego tests of the guardrail bundle, and the trace scripts. The trace tests need git, GNU find and GNU touch, and REQUIRE_ATIME=1 makes a filesystem without access times fail them instead of skipping them. CI also runs shellcheck -s sh internal/tracescript/*.sh scripts/*.sh. The golden files of the example monorepo change with go test ./examples/monorepo -update: read the diff before you commit it.
Validation lists every test layer, and .circleci/continue.yml is the pipeline that runs them.
Keep the repository generic: no customer, vendor-specific or internal names, host names or links. Never print environment variables or secrets in a script, a test or a log.
data.documentation#Documentation: Documentation follows the CircleCI docs style: sentence-case headings, active voice, no contractions, and short sentences. Every docs/*.md page has front matter with page-title, page-audience, and page-description.
data.documentation-site#Documentation site:
The documentation is also a site on GitHub Pages: https://circleci-labs.github.io/smarter-workflows/. CircleCI builds it with Hugo and the Hextra theme, and pushes it to the gh-pages branch. The Markdown stays the only source, and nothing in it is written for the site: README.md is the home page, and site/nav.txt lists the other pages (docs/, the glossary, the composer skill, the compose eval, the demo, this file and the security policy).
Add every new, renamed or removed page to site/nav.txt. site/stage.sh fails on a Markdown file below docs/ that the list misses, and on a listed file that does not exist, so docs-site-build catches a page that would be missing from the sidebar. STAGE_LENIENT=1 turns both errors into warnings while you restructure. A relative link to a file that is a page of the site goes to that page, and a link to any other file of the repository goes to GitHub.
To preview the site, install Hugo extended 0.168.0 and Go (Hugo downloads the theme as a Go module), then run from the repository root:
site/stage.sh cd site && hugo server --bind 127.0.0.1 --baseURL http://127.0.0.1:1313/ Run site/stage.sh again after you change a page. To run the check of the pipeline, install lychee and run (cd site && hugo --minify --panicOnWarning) && site/check.sh. It checks every link and heading anchor of the built site, offline.
The job docs-site-build runs this check on every branch. It reads only the docs and the site sources, so the planner skips it for a change that touches neither. The job docs-site-publish runs on main only, in the workflow docs-site, and pushes the site to gh-pages with the context smarter-workflows-release. Hugo and lychee are pinned by version and SHA-256 in the command docs-site of .circleci/continue.yml: a new version needs its new checksum, from the release page of the tool, in the same change.
A maintainer does this once:
Put a fine-grained token for this repository only, with the repository permission Contents: read and write and nothing else, in the variable GITHUB_TOKEN of the context smarter-workflows-release. Without the variable the job builds and checks the site and publishes nothing.
Restrict the context to this project, and refuse SSH reruns:
circleci context restriction create smarter-workflows-release --org --type project --value circleci context restriction create smarter-workflows-release --org --type expression \ --value 'not job.ssh.enabled and not (pipeline.config_source starts-with "api")' After the first publication, open Settings, Pages, and set Source to Deploy from a branch, the branch to gh-pages and the folder to / (root). GitHub then deploys every push to that branch. There is no workflow file to maintain.

data.opening-a-pull-request#Opening a pull re:
Before you open a pull request:
Discuss large changes in an issue first. Run the checks of Development. Update docs/ when you change a flag, a file format or a default. Write every commit message, and the pull request title, as a Conventional Commit (Commit messages). Check that the diff has no tokens, host names, or customer or vendor names. The repository is public. Add a dependency only when its release is at least 7 days old, and pin it exactly: in go.mod, and by version and checksum for a tool that CI downloads. A pull request that changes only documentation (docs/, site/, Markdown files) runs the docs site build and skips the jobs that do not read those files. That is the planner at work: this repository plans its own pipeline (How it works).
data.reporting-a-bug#Reporting a bug:
Search the existing issues first, and check that you use the latest release or main. Then open a new issue. Include:
The planner version (circleci-smarter version, or the orb version) and the mode you ran in (shadow or select). The plan.md and plan.json that the plan job stores as the artifacts smarter-plan/. They list every job, whether it ran, and why. The files that the change touched, what the plan did, and what you expected. The part of your continue.yml that shows the problem, reduced to the few jobs that matter. Remove tokens, internal host names and private code from everything you paste.
data.requesting-a-feature#Requesting a featur: Open an issue. Describe the problem, and name the command, the flag or the file it affects. For problems in the CircleCI platform, contact CircleCI support instead.

data.reporting-a-vulnerability#Reporting a vu:
Do not open a public issue or pull request for a security vulnerability.
Email security@circleci.com, whether the problem is in Smarter Workflows or in the CircleCI platform. CircleCI’s security team receives the report. The project sets no response target, and CircleCI has no bounty program (process).
For a sensitive report, encrypt the message with the key at https://circleci.com/.well-known/pgp-key.txt.
Include the steps to reproduce, the release or commit, and the planner version (circleci-smarter version).
data.support#Support: Smarter Workflows is a CircleCI Labs project. CircleCI support does not cover it, and field engineers handle bugs and feature requests on a best-effort basis, with no SLA. Use GitHub issues for problems that are not security vulnerabilities.
data.supported-versions#Supported versions: Smarter Workflows is at version 0.x. Fixes land on main and ship in the next release. The code and the design have not been independently reviewed or penetration-tested.
data.what-the-planner-does-with-your-credenti:
Limitations lists the known gaps in detail.
The continuation key (CIRCLE_CONTINUATION_KEY) is read only by circleci-smarter continue. It never prints the key or the request body, only the status code. A trace records the paths of the tracked files that a job read and the directories it listed, not their contents. The impact map is built from those paths. The impact map lives in the project cache, and any branch can write a cache entry. A forged map could make the planner skip jobs. Mandatory jobs and the guardrails do not depend on the map, and every default branch run is a full run. Signing the map on the default branch is planned. The guardrail bundle runs locally in the setup job, against the config that the planner generated. The same bundle can be enforced org-wide as a config policy.

data.consequences#Consequences: The two layers compose: Smarter Workflows skips whole jobs, and Smarter Testing trims the tests inside the jobs that run. The unit of everything here (impact map, plan, report) is a workflow job, never a test.
data.context#Context: Picking tests is already well served: CircleCI Smarter Testing, and the test impact tools from several other vendors. What nobody covers well on CircleCI is which jobs and workflows a change needs, together with their order, approvals, filters and contexts.
data.decision#Decision: Smarter Workflows decides at the level of jobs and workflows. Inside a job it runs, test selection is left to Smarter Testing or to whatever tool the job already uses.

data.consequences#Consequences: Savings come from skipping the parts of the job graph a change cannot reach, such as other services in a monorepo. Shared early jobs, like a repo-wide lint, still run. It assumes a job’s behaviour depends on the repo files it reads. Inputs from outside the repo (the network, the time, secrets, upstream images) are covered by the full run on the default branch, by mandatory jobs, and by extra inputs a project declares by hand. A project may already use a no-op job that nothing requires as its one required status check (a gatekeeper, such as all-tests-passed). The planner always keeps it, and cuts what it waits for to the jobs that stay, or to the gate, so its check always reports and never passes early. A job that does not run on the branch (its own filters leave it out, or all the jobs it requires are left out) is never selected, even when it is mandatory. The planner does not edit the project’s filters or requirements to force a job. It leaves such a job out, and a mandatory one gets a warning. It drops a requires name only when it names a job that does not run, which CircleCI ignores anyway. Skipping a job on confidence alone, without proof, is out of scope until shadow-mode data shows recall of at least 99% for that job.
data.context#Context: A skipped job that would have failed (a miss) costs more than an extra job that passes. Path filters miss when their globs drift from what jobs really read. Learned models miss when history is thin. GitHub branch protection also waits forever on a required check whose job was skipped.
data.decision#Decision: Every job runs unless the planner can show that the change touches none of its inputs: no changed file is among the files the job read in the last traced full run; no added or deleted file sits in a directory the job listed. These always run: jobs with no trace, or an incomplete trace; mandatory jobs; every ancestor (requires) of a selected job, approvals included. A full run happens: on the default branch and on tags; for scheduled pipelines; when the change touches the pipeline definition (.circleci/** by default); when there is no impact map, the diff base cannot be found, or the planner hits any error; when the head commit asks for one. Every decision layer added later (history, models) can only add jobs. Every workflow the planner prunes ends in one gate job, smarter-gate, which requires every selected job that will run. It is a no-op job (type: no-op), so it costs no credits. So the workflow always exists and its check always reports: GitHub App projects report one check per workflow, and branch protection requires that check; with per-job statuses, branch protection requires the gate alone.

data.consequences#Consequences: No ML, no per-language code, no hand-written globs. The map explains itself: “this job read these files”. noatime filesystems, busybox find and non-Linux executors give incomplete traces, so those jobs always run. Because a read is “atime past the epoch”, an input that is read and then rewritten in the same job (a formatter run with -w) still counts as read. Traces still miss inputs from outside the repo: see ADR 2 for how those are covered. Cache entries can expire (default retention) and can be written by any branch. A missing map means a full run. Mandatory jobs and guardrails do not depend on the map. Signing the map on the default branch is planned hardening.
data.context#Context:
Smarter Testing builds an impact map on the default branch, then uses it on other branches to pick the tests a change affects. This project wants the same loop for jobs:
a full run on the default branch rebuilds the map; branches use it; a merge triggers the next full run, which rebuilds it again. A job’s equivalent of test coverage is the set of repo files it reads. There are several ways to record that:
Hand-written globs go stale. Language analyzers need one per ecosystem, and miss scripts and config files. strace and LD_PRELOAD are slow, and Go binaries bypass libc. fanotify and eBPF need privileges that Docker jobs do not have. Access times (atime) cost nothing. Under the usual relatime mount option, the first read after a write always updates a file’s atime. A freshly checked-out file has atime equal to mtime, so a file that was read has atime greater than mtime.
data.decision#Decision: On full runs of the default branch, the planner adds two steps to every job of the pruned workflow: Right after checkout, a reset step sets the atime of every tracked file and directory to the epoch, because checkout itself reads every file. It also probes that atime works on that filesystem. A post-step records the tracked files and the directories whose atime has since moved past the epoch: the ones the job read or listed. A job whose filesystem fails the probe gets an incomplete trace. A final job merges the traces into the impact map. It saves the map to the project cache under a key derived from the commit SHA. On other branches, the planner restores the map for the merge-base commit, falling back to the newest map. Only green full runs produce a map.

data.decision#Decision: Select mode (v0.1): the catalog is the project’s own full continuation config (.circleci/continue.yml). The planner prunes those workflows and keeps the order, approvals, filters and contexts the team wrote. Planner settings (mode, mandatory jobs, full-run paths, extra inputs) are parameters of the orb job, not a new file. Shared catalogs are orbs, pinned to exact versions: the only job-level units that cannot change underneath you. URL orbs are allowed only when pinned to a commit SHA. data.consequences#Consequences: One language and one binary, with no runtime dependencies in the planner job. The trace collector stays a small POSIX shell script, so jobs need no extra binary.
data.context#Context: The tool has to be easy to adopt in production if product teams like it. The circleci CLI dispatches circleci to a binary named circleci-; Smarter Testing’s testsuite is one such extension. CircleCI’s policy engine is a public Go library (circle-policy-agent), so a Go binary can evaluate policies exactly the way the service does.
data.decision#Decision: Ship a single static Go binary, circleci-smarter, that can be called directly or as circleci smarter. It embeds the trace collector script, and links circle-policy-agent for the pre-flight. The orb downloads a pinned, checksummed release. Until releases exist, it builds from source.

data.consequences#Consequences: Guardrails work on every plan, Scale or not. On Scale they are also enforced server-side. Policies cannot read parameters as values, so the planner emits literal config and never adds parameters. Compose mode will reuse the same loop, with an agent doing the repair.
data.context#Context: CircleCI config policies also evaluate the continuation config. Server-side enforcement needs the Scale plan, and a continuation the server rejects fails the pipeline after the setup job has already spent its one continuation.
data.decision#Decision: The planner runs the project’s policy bundle locally, against the config it generated, using circle-policy-agent. Policies in the bundle tag violations the planner can fix with a machine-readable code, e.g. [smarter:require-job=security-scan]. The planner applies the fix and plans again, up to 3 times. A violation it cannot fix turns the plan into a full run, which is checked again. If even the full config fails, the setup job fails with the violations listed, without continuing. The same bundle can be pushed as org policy, limited to the projects that opt in, starting with soft-fail.

data.consequences#Consequences: Monorepo-sized maps fit in cache and decode in sub-second time on developer hardware (see docs/benchmarks-perf.md). Path tables must stay sorted and deduplicated; corrupt index blobs fail closed at parse time. Cache artifacts change extension; operators with only v1 files still work until the next default-branch map build.
data.context#Context: Impact map v1 stores every repo path verbatim in each job’s files and dirs arrays. On large monorepos the JSON grows with the number of job×path pairs (roughly jobs × average reads), blows past the 16 MiB parse cap, and takes seconds to decode. A realistic shape is thousands of jobs each reading a large fraction of tens or hundreds of thousands of unique paths.
data.decision#Decision: On-disk format v2 (still JSON, gzip-compressed as impact-map.json.gz): Sorted files and dirs tables: each repo path appears once. Per job, file_idx and dir_idx are standard base64 blobs of sorted delta varints over table indices (first index absolute, later indices encode the gap from the previous one). Metadata unchanged: revision, created_at, method, and per-job complete and nodes. Why delta varints instead of bitsets: Indices are dense when jobs read many files but sparse when they read few; delta varints are small in the common case, need no third-party format, and decode in one pass with strict bounds. Roaring or raw bitsets win when sets are extremely sparse across a huge table; this workload is usually “many indices per job out of a shared table”, where varints are simpler and fast enough. Writers (map build, the trace map job) emit v2 gzip only. Readers accept v1 JSON (legacy cache) and v2 gzip; plan tries impact-map.json.gz then impact-map.json. Caps (oversize or malformed → full run): compressed file ≤ 64 MiB; decompressed JSON ≤ 256 MiB; when compressed size < 64 KiB, decompressed must be ≤ 32× compressed (zip-bomb guard); ≤ 4096 jobs; ≤ 200_000 file table entries; ≤ 50_000 dir table entries; ≤ 100_000 indices per job per table; job names ≤ 256 chars. v1 maps keep the former 16 MiB uncompressed cap.

data.the-loop#The loop:
push to main ──► setup: plan job ──► full run, every job traced ──► smarter-impact-map ──► project cache │ push to a branch ──► setup: plan job ◄── impact map for the merge-base (or the newest) ◄────────┘ │ ├─ changed files (merge-base..HEAD) × impact map → which jobs the change can reach ├─ + mandatory jobs, + ancestors, + workspace consumers ├─ guardrails pre-flight (policies/), repair or full run └─ continue: pruned workflow + smarter-gate The default branch always gets a full run. The planner adds two steps to each job:
a step right after checkout that resets file access times; a post-step that records which tracked files the job read and which directories it listed. A last job, smarter-impact-map, merges these traces into the impact map and saves it to the project cache under the commit’s SHA. A branch gets a plan. The plan job:
finds the merge-base with the default branch; restores the impact map for that commit, or the newest map; compares the changed files with what each job read. A job runs when the change touches one of its inputs, or a directory it listed gains or loses a file. Mandatory jobs always run. So do:
the ancestors (requires) of every job that runs; jobs that consume a workspace produced by a job that runs; jobs with no trace; job groups: an entry that names a group under job-groups runs as one unit, since v0.1 does not look inside it. Some entries run no steps: an approval (type: approval, on the entry or in the job’s definition), a no-op job (type: no-op) and a release job (type: release). They are never traced and have no inputs, so the jobs around them decide. An approval or a no-op job stays when a job that runs requires it. A release job stays when a job it requires runs: it tracks that job’s release. A no-op job that nothing requires, such as an all-tests-passed that you use as your required status check, always stays: it waits only for the jobs that stay, or for smarter-gate when none of the jobs it waited for does, so it never passes before the selected jobs have.
A job that your own filters keep off the branch, or whose required jobs they all keep off it, does not run there whatever the change is, even when it is mandatory. The plan leaves it out and says so in a warning. A requirement on a job that does not run is ignored, as in CircleCI, and the plan drops it.
Guardrails. The planner checks the config it generated against the Rego bundle in policies/, using CircleCI’s own policy engine (circle-policy-agent).
If a mandatory job is missing, it adds the job and checks again. Any other hard violation turns the plan into a full run. The gate. Every planned workflow ends with smarter-gate, which waits for every selected job. The workflow always runs, even when only the gate is left.
The gate is a no-op job (smarter-gate: {type: no-op}): no executor and no steps, so it costs no credits and starts no container. It is CircleCI’s gatekeeper pattern for one required status check. It succeeds when every job it requires succeeds. CircleCI’s GitHub App reports one check per workflow (e.g. ci - ): make that check required. If you use per-job status checks, require smarter-gate. Either way, a PR never waits on a skipped job.
data.tools-for-agents#Tools for agents:
Two commands let an agent (or a person) read a pipeline and check a layout of it, with no plan and no impact map needed:
circleci-smarter catalog --config .circleci/continue.yml --map impact-map.json.gz prints the jobs of a workflow as JSON: each one’s kind, executor, contexts, filters, requirements, workspace use and, with a map, how much of the repository it read. circleci-smarter layout check --config composed.yml --catalog catalog.json --policy-bundle policies --mandatory security-scan --restricted-contexts deploy checks how the jobs of a workflow wait for each other, and reports each problem with a code and a hint on how to fix it: a requires that points nowhere, a cycle, a workspace attached before it is persisted, a restricted context with no approval before it, a missing mandatory job, a gate that is not a no-op job or does not wait for every job that runs, and an approval that a branch filter can leave out. It exits 3 when there are errors. A plan the planner writes has a no-op gate and no structural problem that its input did not have. The spec has the formats.

One planned workflow. Other workflows in continue.yml pass through with the same meaning. YAML anchors, aliases and merge keys are expanded everywhere, and formatting such as indentation may change. Job groups are one opaque unit. An entry that names a group under job-groups always runs, with everything it requires, and is not traced. Its serial-group and the group are kept as written. The planner and layout check do not look inside a group: a restricted context used by a job inside one is not seen, and a job outside the group cannot require a job inside it. A release job (type: release) is never traced. It stays when a job it requires runs, and then so does everything it requires. Matrix jobs always run. Orb jobs are traced only with --trace-orb-jobs: it adds a checkout and a reset as pre-steps, so it only suits orb jobs that check out the repo. Without it they always run. Self-hosted runners and other opaque Linux executors (machine: true without an image, namespace/resource_class, parameterised executors) are not traced unless you list them with --trace-jobs (comma-separated name globs). Windows and macOS entries are never traced, even when listed. Plan reports explain untraced jobs in plan.json (trace_coverage) and plan.md, so you can see unknown executors, missing checkout, job groups, matrix jobs and the like. Expression filters (string filters) are reported, and left out of the gate. Workflow when/unless are evaluated only when every value is known from --parameters, --branch, --tag and --trigger-type. Unsupported forms still mean a full run. When the condition is false, the workflow is not pruned and gets no gate (CircleCI skips it). A job that requires only filtered-out jobs by a status (- deploy: failed, with deploy filtered out on the branch) may or may not run, so the plan cannot leave it out or drop its requirement: it is a full run. Spec v0.1: The v0.1 specification of Smarter Workflows: the CLI contract, the file formats, the planning algorithm, the guardrail bundle, and the tests that gate a merge. Glossary: The words this project uses, and what each one means.

The words this project uses, and what each one means. There are no implementation details here. For those, see the spec and the decisions.
Change The set of files a branch changes, compared with the commit it branched from on the default branch. Planner The step in the setup workflow that decides, for one change, which jobs of the pipeline run. Plan What the planner decides for one pipeline: the jobs that run, the jobs that are skipped and the reason for each, and the continuation config that carries this out. Full run A pipeline that runs every job. The default branch, scheduled pipelines, changes to the pipeline definition, and any case the planner is unsure about all get a full run. Impact map For each job, the files it read and the directories it listed during the last full run on the default branch. It is rebuilt after every green full run, and branches use it to see which jobs a change can affect. Trace The record of the files one job read, taken at the end of the job. The impact map is built from traces. Inputs (of a job) The files and directories in a job’s trace. A job whose inputs a change does not touch is a candidate to skip. Shadow mode The planner makes and reports a plan, but every job still runs. Shadow mode measures what select mode would save, and what it would miss. Select mode The planner runs only the jobs its plan selects. Compose mode A later mode: an agent builds jobs and workflows from approved building blocks, within the guardrails. Mandatory job A job that runs in every pipeline, whatever the change, such as a security scan. Gate job The last job of the workflow, which waits for every selected job. It always runs, so a branch protection rule can require it alone, even when other jobs are skipped. It is a no-op job: no executor, no steps, no credits. No-op job A job defined with type: no-op. It runs nothing and costs no credits. It succeeds when the jobs it requires succeed. Gatekeeper A no-op job that no other job requires, which a project uses as its one required status check (for example all-tests-passed). Select mode always keeps it, and cuts what it waits for to the jobs that stay. Layout How the jobs of one workflow wait for each other (requires, approvals, filters), as opposed to what each job does. layout check reports what is wrong with it. Guardrail A config policy that every generated config must pass. Examples: mandatory jobs, contexts allowed only on certain jobs and branches, an approval before a deploy. Pre-flight The planner’s own check of its config against the guardrails, before it continues the pipeline. Repair A change the planner makes to its plan so that it passes a guardrail, such as adding a missing mandatory job. A failure it cannot repair turns the plan into a full run. Miss A job the plan skipped (or, in shadow mode, would have skipped) that would have failed. Savings The credits and minutes that skipped jobs did not spend. Catalog The jobs, commands, executors and orbs the planner may pick from. In select mode, the catalog is the project’s own pipeline config.

data.cli-contract-circleci-smarter-command#CL:
Exit codes for all commands:
0: ok; 1: fatal error; 2: usage error; 3: the guardrails failed and the pipeline must not continue (plan, policy check), or the layout has errors (layout check).
data.continue#continue: circleci-smarter continue --config PATH [--parameters PATH] Reads CIRCLE_CONTINUATION_KEY, and CIRCLECI_API_HOST (default https://circleci.com). POSTs to /api/v2/pipeline/continue. Retries on 429 and 5xx: 3 tries, waiting 1, 2 then 4 s. Never prints the key or the request body. It prints only the status code.
data.goal#Goal: A setup workflow runs the circleci-smarter planner. For a branch, the planner prunes the planned workflow of .circleci/continue.yml down to the jobs the change can reach. It checks the result against the guardrails and continues the pipeline. On the default branch it runs everything, traces each job’s file reads, and rebuilds the impact map.
data.guardrail-bundle-policies#Guardrail bund: package org, using CircleCI’s policy conventions (policy_name, enable_hard) and data.circleci.config helpers where they fit. The settings are constants at the top of the file, for projects to edit. Rules: Required jobs (security-scan by default) are present in every workflow of a non-setup config. The message carries the repair code. Restricted contexts (e.g. deploy): allowed only on listed jobs, only on listed branches or on tags, and only downstream of an approval job (type: approval on the entry, or in the job’s definition). Resource classes come from an allowlist. Check the source jobs, and _compiled_ when it is present. A no-op job has no executor, so it is not checked. Registry orbs are pinned to an exact x.y.z. URL orbs carry a 40-hex commit SHA. A continuation config does not declare setup: true. Tests: Rego _test.rego files plus Go fixture tests through internal/policy. Locally there is no _compiled_, so rules must cope with it being absent.

data.what-an-entry-runs#What an entry runs:
The planner reads what each entry of W runs from the job’s definition (jobs: of the config), and from the top-level job-groups:
Kind Written as Selected by job a job that runs steps (type: build, the default) its inputs (step 3), or the closure (step 4) approval type: approval on the entry, or in the job’s definition the closure only no-op type: no-op in the job’s definition: no executor, no steps, no credits the closure. One that no entry requires is a gatekeeper, and is always kept (step 7) release type: release in the job’s definition (plan_name): it tracks the release that a deploy job planned any job it requires being selected (step 4) job group the name of a group under the top-level job-groups, used as a job nothing: it always runs, as one unit (step 3) orb job a job that the config does not define its inputs; no map entry means it runs An approval, a no-op job and a release job run no steps, so they are never traced and have no inputs. A job group is not looked into: v0.1 plans it as one opaque unit. A serial-group key of an entry, and the job-groups key, are never touched: they come out as they went in.
Full run. Plan a full run when any of these holds:
--force-full; the branch is the default branch, or there is a tag; the trigger type is schedule; the head commit asks for one; there is no base, or no usable map; a changed path (old or new) matches --full-run-paths; W has a when or unless that cannot be evaluated (see below). When when/unless can be evaluated and is false for this pipeline (workflow_runs in the plan report), the workflow is left untouched (no gate, no pruning) and every job is reported as skipped. 1b. Workflow when/unless. After the full-run checks above, evaluate W’s when and unless when every value they use is known: literal booleans; << pipeline.parameters.NAME >>; logic statements and, or, not, equal and matches; and the string expression form (pipeline.git.branch == "main", !=, and/or/not, starts-with). Known pipeline values come from --branch, --tag, --trigger-type and --parameters. If evaluation succeeds and the workflow would not run, stop (step 1, last bullet). If any subexpression is unknown or unsupported, treat it like step 1 (full run). If it would run, continue. Changes. Run git diff --name-status -M -z .
Renames count as the old path deleted plus the new path added. Paths that match --ignore-paths are dropped before step 3. Direct selection. For each entry J of W (its effective name is name: if set, else the job reference). An entry that does not run on this branch or tag (step 5) is never selected, whatever else holds, so it never seeds step 4:
approval and no-op entries are decided by the closure in step 4, and so are release entries (by the rule there). None has a trace, so none has inputs of its own, and --mandatory does not force them. The exception is a gatekeeper: a no-op entry that no entry requires, that waits for success only, and that runs on this branch or tag (step 5). It is kept, with the reason “kept: a no-op gatekeeper”, whatever else is selected. It selects nothing: it is not part of the closure; a job group entry runs, with the reason “job group: runs as one unit, as v0.1 does not look inside it” (and it is not traced, step 8); a matrix entry runs; a mandatory job runs. If step 5 says it does not run here, the planner leaves it out and records a warning; it does not force a job to run; a job whose extra inputs match a changed path runs; a job with no map entry, or an incomplete one, runs; a job that read a changed file runs; for an added or deleted path P, J runs if J listed the parent directory of P. It also runs if J listed any ancestor directory whose direct child on P’s path is a directory that is new at the head or gone from the base (use git ls-tree at the base and the head); otherwise J is skipped, with the reason “inputs unchanged”. Closure.
Every requires ancestor of a selected job is selected, approvals and no-op jobs included, except an ancestor that does not run (step 5). CircleCI ignores a requirement on such a job, and step 7 drops it. So an approval, or a no-op job that some entry requires, is skipped when no selected job requires it, with the reason “no selected job requires this approval” (or “no-op job”). A release entry is selected when any job it requires is selected (“tracks the release of X”); its other requirements are selected like those of any selected job. Otherwise it is skipped: “none of the jobs it requires is selected”. Producers are local jobs with persist_to_workspace; consumers are local jobs with attach_workspace. Steps in a local command, and in the entry’s own pre-steps and post-steps, count. Orb jobs and job groups count as both. When a selected producer K has a consumer J downstream of it, J is selected. Repeat both rules until nothing changes. Will it run? Evaluate filters for the current branch or tag:
CircleCI semantics: string or list, and /regex/ is a full match; jobs do not run on tags without a matching tags.only; expression (string) filters are unknown; they are reported; this is CircleCI’s own rule (configuration reference, requires): a requirement on a job that does not run is ignored, but a job whose requirements are all filtered out does not run either. So a job runs only if its own filters allow it and, when it has requirements, at least one of them runs, all the way up the graph. A job with one filtered-out requirement and one that runs still runs, after the one that runs; a requirement on a job status other than success (- build: failed), or on a name that no entry answers to, makes the job unknown, unless its own filters already say it does not run. Gate. Add the job smarter-gate:
its definition is smarter-gate: {type: no-op}, with no executor and no steps, so it costs no credits. This is CircleCI’s documented gatekeeper pattern for one required status check. It needs a workflow entry like any job, and it fails only if a job it requires fails; its workflow entry requires every selected job that will certainly run (step 5 says yes), except approvals, no-op jobs (they run no steps, so they fail only with the jobs they require, which the gate waits for) and jobs downstream of an approval (an approval that step 5 says does not run is not there to wait for). A selected job that is unknown is left out, with a warning that names it: a job whose filters cannot be evaluated, or smarter-gate does not wait for X: it requires a job status other than success (a job that waits for a failure may never run, and the gate would wait for it for ever); if nothing else is selected, W contains only the gate. Emit.
Select mode: remove the skipped entries from W. From the entries that stay, drop a requires name only when it names a removed job that does not run (step 5): CircleCI ignores it, so the meaning is the same. Never drop the last name of a list, and never a name that is a job that runs: that could change what runs. If the plan would, it is an internal error: a full run. A gatekeeper (step 3) stays in select mode, and its requires is cut to the entries that stay: every name of an entry that is removed goes, whether that entry would run or not, and the items that stay keep their form. If none stays, it requires the gate, so that it never passes before the selected jobs have. A project that makes its gatekeeper (say all-tests-passed) the required status check keeps one that reports. A gatekeeper that does not run on this branch (all it requires is filtered out) is left out like any entry that does not run. Shadow mode: keep every entry. The report still shows what select mode would have skipped. Every other part of the config keeps its meaning: other workflows, jobs, orbs, comments and key order. Never add pipeline parameters. Emit literals only. Trace (full runs on the default branch, when --trace resolves to on):
On every entry of W that is a local Linux job (docker, or machine with a Linux image), append post-steps. An approval, a no-op job, a release job, a job group and a matrix entry get none. Orb jobs are included only with --trace-orb-jobs; without it, an orb entry gets no pre-steps and no post-steps. A pre-steps or post-steps key with no value is an empty list. An entry whose pre-steps or post-steps is not a list gets no trace, with a warning: the others are traced, and since it has no map entry, later plans always run it. a run step named smarter: collect trace, with when: always, shell: /bin/sh, and as its command the embedded collect-trace.sh; persist_to_workspace with root /tmp/smarter and paths [traces]. If the spike (W3) shows that checkout itself reads files, also insert a step right after the first checkout of the job: a top-level step, or right after a local command invocation whose definition contains checkout (including nested commands, up to a depth limit). For checkout: {path: X}, the reset and collect steps get CIRCLE_WORKING_DIRECTORY set to that path. The planner cannot reach the checkout inside an orb job, so with --trace-orb-jobs an orb entry gets pre-steps [checkout, ] instead: it checks out first, then resets, and the orb job’s own checkout follows. Jobs with no checkout are not traced. The plan report lists every workflow job in trace_coverage, with a reason when it is not traced (unknown executor, no checkout, job group, matrix, orb without --trace-orb-jobs, and so on). Add the job smarter-impact-map. It requires every traced entry that is not downstream of an approval. Its steps: write .smarter-version (the planner’s own version, as a literal); restore_cache with key smarter-bin-v1-{{ checksum ".smarter-version" }}-{{ arch }}; attach_workspace at /tmp/smarter; map build; write .smarter-key ($CIRCLE_SHA1); save_cache with key <--map-key-prefix>-{{ checksum ".smarter-key" }} (by default smarter-impact-v1-{{ checksum ".smarter-key" }}) for /tmp/smarter/impact-map.json.gz; store_artifacts. Guardrails (when --policy-bundle is set):
policy.Check the emitted config. For a hard violation carrying [smarter:require-job=NAME], force NAME and plan again (at most 3 rounds). Forcing selects the job; it cannot make a job run that step 5 says does not run here, so the violation stays and step 3 applies. If hard violations are left, plan a full run and check again. If that still fails, exit 3. Soft violations go into the report as warnings.

data: Smarter Workflows runs inside a customer’s CircleCI project: a setup workflow plans which jobs to run on a branch, then continues the pipeline. This page is generic; it does not describe any one org’s policies.
data.assets#Assets: Repository source — integrity and confidentiality as for any CI job. Continuation config — defines the jobs that run after setup; may reference contexts and images. Continuation key — secret that authorizes continuing the pipeline (environment variable). Impact map — gzip JSON (v2) or legacy JSON (v1) in the project cache describing which files each job read on a past full run. Plan report — plan.json / plan.md with job decisions and diffs. Trace scripts — shell embedded in customer job configs (reset-atime.sh, collect-trace.sh). Policy bundle — Rego guardrails evaluated before continuation.
data.cli-output-paths#CLI output paths:
Threat: Odd --out / --report-dir values or world-readable continuation config.
Mitigations: Null-byte paths rejected. Continuation config written 0600; plan report files 0640 in a 0750 directory; impact map 0640.
Residual risk: Paths are absolute or relative as the operator gives them; the CLI does not sandbox writes outside the workspace.
data.continuation-client#Continuation client:
Threat: Key or config leaks via logs, redirects, or error messages.
Mitigations: Errors name HTTP status only. Response body not logged. No redirect follow (key stays on intended host). HTTPS required except loopback. Config size capped at 8 MiB. Key redaction if ever present in an error string.
Residual risk: Operator misconfiguration (HTTP to a non-loopback host) is rejected at client construction.
data.forged-or-hostile-impact-map#Forged or h:
Threat: A branch writes a cache entry claiming jobs did not read files they actually use, so the planner skips work.
Mitigations: Mandatory jobs always run. Guardrails do not depend on the map. Unusable paths mark a job incomplete (it runs). Oversized or malformed maps are rejected (full run). v2 bounds compressed and decompressed bytes, table sizes, job count, and per-job index counts at parse time (v1 keeps a 16 MiB cap). See ADR 7.
Residual risk: A plausible forged map can still skip optional jobs until signing on the default branch (limitations). Operators should treat map cache as hint data, not proof.
data.injection-via-config-map-or-yaml-emissio:
Threat: Job names, paths, or parameters break out of generated YAML or inlined shell.
Mitigations: Gate and map key prefixes match a safe identifier regex. Map job steps quote version and binary path for /bin/sh. Trace scripts are static literals (no customer interpolation). Embedded scripts avoid tabs and CircleCI template syntax. Job names with expressions trigger a full run.
Residual risk: Customer-authored job definitions in the catalog are unchanged; only added smarter steps are constrained.
data.policy-bundle-loading#Policy bundle load:
Threat: Symlink or path traversal loads Rego from outside the bundle directory.
Mitigations: Walk stays under bundle root; symlinks skipped; *_test.rego ignored. Hostile YAML in config fails Check without executing customer code.
Residual risk: Evaluated config is still customer YAML interpreted by circle-policy-agent; bundle should be operator-maintained.

data.trace-scripts-in-customer-jobs#Trace scr:
Threat: Malicious repo layout or environment breaks quoting, leaks secrets, fails the job, or exhausts resources.
Mitigations: set +e; always exit 0. No network. No printing environment variables. CIRCLE_JOB hashed for filenames; job text sanitized to one line in the TSV. Temp dirs under .git. GNU tool probes fail closed to “unsupported trace”. Hostile path tests in scripts/test-trace.sh.
Residual risk: Very large repos cost time during find/git traversal; tracing is only on the default branch by default.

data.bugs-that-validation-found-and-fixed#Bug: A job’s requires on a filtered-out job: the planner now follows CircleCI’s documented rule. A filtered-out requirement is ignored, unless every requirement is filtered out. YAML anchors, aliases and merge keys are expanded before pruning. Before the fix, they could leave dangling aliases or duplicate injected steps. A null pre-steps or post-steps is an empty list. Before the fix, it dropped the whole trace. A fallback full run still gets the gate and tracing. The gate says when it does not wait for a job with a status requirement. In CI only: git’s background maintenance made temp-repo cleanup flaky; the orb is now validated without an API token; some orgs’ config policies allow only exact image tags, so the language images of the pipeline carry a tag and no digest.

data.end-to-end-scenarios#End-to-end scenario:
Twenty-one scenarios on two targets: the demo monorepo (16 scenarios, 13 jobs, select mode) and this repository (5 scenarios, 8 jobs). Each scenario ran three times on the same base commit (63 pipeline runs total). Every run checked the jobs that ran (besides smarter-gate), guardrail outcome where relevant, and the continued workflow’s GitHub check conclusion.
First batch (63 runs): 57 passed the job-set check. Six did not:
Scenario What went wrong self-policies (×3) The scenario expected only go-test, policy-test, release-dry-run, and security-scan. Adding policies/NOTES.md also satisfies build, go-lint, and e2e-plan, which list policies/ or depend on build’s workspace — by design. self-orb (×3) The change step edited orb/orb.yml, which no longer exists; the orb lives under orb/src/@orb.yml. The branch was never pushed. After fixing the scenarios: self-policies was rerun once with the expanded expected job set (build, e2e-plan, go-lint, go-test, policy-test, release-dry-run, security-scan) and passed. self-orb was rerun once against orb/src/@orb.yml; the planner ran orb-validate and security-scan only (Go inputs unchanged), matching the corrected expectation. The first batch therefore reported 57/63 job-set matches; with the two definition fixes verified on real pipelines, all 21 scenarios are accounted for. See the savings table in Benchmarks.
The two worker-test matrix jobs always run on the demo target in v0.1.
